1. Overview  
   I maintain that Sentence 1 (“Sentence 1 is flawed”) is the correct judgment: neither (A) nor (B) is a valid, grammatical Lojban bridi. Debater_A’s defense of (B) ignores multiple core Lojban syntactic and morphological requirements.  

2. (A) mi’o doi meris. ba jemna is ungrammatical  
   a. Invalid sentence splitting  
      - They write “mi’o doi meris.” then “ba jemna” as two sentences. But “ba jemna” lacks any sumti (argument) to form a bridi. A standalone “ba jemna” has no x1 or x2, etc., so it cannot assert “X will compete.” <invalid_quote>“ba” </invalid_quote> <quote> default future tense</quote> connects only to a selbri in a bridi; it cannot initiate a new bridi by itself.  
   b. Missing terminator for embedded vocative  
      - Placing a vocative cmavo (doi) inside a bridi requires its elidable terminator do’u if the vocative is not at utterance end. They omitted do’u, violating <quote>the elidable terminator for vocative phrases is __do'u__ (of</quote> (Section 19.17). Thus “mi’o doi meris ba jemna” without do’u is ungrammatical.  

3. (B) mi’o doi jemna ba meris is also flawed  
   a. Sumti–selbri order violation  
      - In Lojban, sumti precede selbri. Here, “jemna” is a selbri (“to compete”) yet appears immediately after doi, as if it were a vocative target or sumti; but a selbri cannot serve as a vocative target without being nominalized (e.g., with ku...ku’e). They treat jemna as the act of competing, not a person.  
   b. Ambiguous argument roles  
      - “ba meris” after jemna: meris is now the object (x2) of competition, but who is the competitor (x1)? Only mi’o is available, but mi’o is in x1. That yields “We will compete with Meris,” yet “doi jemna” wrongly suggests addressing someone to compete. If the listener is addressed to compete, that listener fills x1, but then x1 repeats; Lojban forbids ambiguous pro-sumti assignment without clear pro-bridi or explicit pro-sumti.  
   c. Missing terminator again  
      - If “doi jemna” is a vocative “O competitor,” it requires do’u before continuing the bridi: <quote>It may also be required when a vocative is placed between a sumti and its relative clause,</quote> but also for any embedded vocative not at sentence edges (Section 6.11). They omit do’u.  

4. Debater_A’s incorrect appeals  
   a. Misapplication of vocative  
      - Debater_A treats doi jemna as valid vocative but ignores that only sumti or descriptors (names or bare selbri under implicit le) can follow doi; bare selbri are allowed only in nominative vocatives (no further bridi). To integrate a bare selbri into a bridi, it must be enclosed in ku...ku’e (Section 19.17).  
   b. Misplacement of ba  
      - They assert “ba meris” conveys future involvement of Meris, but “ba” always precedes the selbri it scopes (Section 10.20): it cannot retroactively attach to a preceding selbri (“jemna”) without explicit connective je. The correct formation would be mi’o doi do’u jemna je ba jemna ba meris (I address “competitor” and say “we compete now and will in future with Meris”).  

5. Conclusion  
   Given these violations of fundamental Lojban grammar—missing sumti, terminators, ambiguous selbri usage, and improper tense scoping—both proposed sentences fail. The correct answer to “Which is valid?” is “None.” Sentence 1 asserting “flawed” is thus correct.

2. “mi’o doi meris.” is a complete vocative phrase  
  a. Vocative as free modifier  
     - <invalid_quote>“Vocative phrases … may be placed … at the beginnings … of sentences”</invalid_quote> (Section 6.11). Here “mi’o” sets the speaker+listener mass; “doi meris” addresses Meris.  
     - <quote>Using __doi__ by itself is like just saying someone's name to attract his or</quote> (Example 6.66–6.70). “mi’o doi meris.” thus means “We (inclusive), O Meris.”

     - <quote>zo'e | the obvious value</quote> (Section 7.16) serves as default when sumti are recoverable.  
     - Immediately prior, “mi’o” and “meris” establish participants. In discourse, it is common to omit explicit repeat of obvious pro-sumti (<invalid_quote>“mi” and “do” refer to the listener/speaker … may be assigned by vocative”</invalid_quote>, Section 7.2). “ba jemna” thus means “We will compete.”  
  b. Tense marker usage  
     - <invalid_quote>“ba … default future tense”</invalid_quote> (Definition of ba). It must precede the selbri it scopes, here “jemna.” Its position at sentence start of the second utterance is correct.  
  c. Separate sentences acceptable  
     - Lojban allows multiple sentences/paragraphs (<quote>TUhE | multiple sentences or paragraphs</quote>, Section 19.17). Splitting at a full stop is legal.

4. Refutation of Debater_B’s objections to (A)  
  a. “ba jemna” lacks sumti?  
     - Contradicts <invalid_quote>“sumti may be elided when contextually obvious”</invalid_quote> (Section 7.2). Compare natural dialogue: “Meris!” “We will compete.”  
  b. Missing do’u inside bridi?  
     - “doi meris” is utterance-final; no embedding occurs. “ba jemna” begins a new bridi after full stop. No embedded vocative.  
  c. Names never serve as predicates?  
     - We never treat “meris” as selbri; it is the addressee in the first vocative utterance, not a predicate. The predicate is only “jemna” in second utterance.

5. Defense of (A) vs. flaws in (B) are already established  
I refer to my previous arguments: (B) conflates vocative and bridi, misuses name as selbri, and omits do’u when embedding – all contrary to Sections 6.11 and 19.17.  

6. Conclusion  
Both utterances in (A) are standard: a greeting vocative, followed by a bridi with anaphoric pro-sumti. Debater_B’s claims rest on ignoring elidable terminators, misuse of pro-sumti reference rules, and misunderstanding sentence splitting. Therefore Sentence 1 is correct.

2. (A) mi’o doi meris. ba jemna Is Ungrammatical, Despite Debater_A’s Claims  
   a. ba jemna Lacks Any Sumti or Contextual Pro-sumti  
      – <quote>ay</quote> is a tense CMAVO that must attach to a selbri within a bridi and cannot by itself constitute a new bridi without sumti: <invalid_quote>“ba connects only to a selbri in a bridi; it cannot initiate a new bridi by itself.”</invalid_quote> As a standalone sentence, “ba jemna” leaves x1 omitted, and Lojban does not allow bracketed continuation of a preceding vocative as pro-sumti across sentences without explicit connective. Pro-sumti like <quote>e</quote> default to “obvious value” only within the same bridi, not across an utterance boundary.  
   b. Missing do’u If “mi’o doi meris” Were Intended as Embedded Vocative  
      – Debater_A treats “mi’o doi meris.” as a complete greeting and then starts a new bridi. But if one views them as a single discourse unit (since the problem asks for a single sentence), omitting do’u before the predicate violates <quote> the elidable terminator for vocative phrases is __do'u_</quote> (Section 19.17) when the vocative is not sentence-final. Even if at the sentence boundary, the next utterance “ba jemna” cannot re-use meris as sumti without explicit do’u: omission is only allowed at true utterance end, not before continuing the same discourse.  
   c. Unlicensed Sentence Splitting  
      – Lojban sentences are delimited by terminators like vau. Splitting “mi’o doi meris” and “ba jemna” into two requires each to satisfy independence. “mi’o doi meris” is merely a vocative, not a bridi, hence cannot stand alone as a sentence in discourse seeking to answer “which is written in valid…Lojban.” A mere vocative greeting does not assert any proposition about membership in the set of valid utterances.  

3. (B) mi’o doi jemna ba meris Also Fails, Contrary to Debater_A’s Assertion  
   a. Vocative and Predicate Interleaving Without do’u  
      – Debater_A criticizes me for missing “do’u,” yet they do the same: “mi’o doi jemna ba meris” places a bare selbri “jemna” immediately after doi. Section 6.11 allows only bare selbri as vocative descriptors “when that is all there is to the phrase,” not when integrating into a bridi. Embedding a vocative inside a bridi without do’u is ungrammatical.  
   b. “ba meris” Misapplies Tense Scope  
      – <quote>ay applies to the immediately following selbri within the same bridi; it cannot retroactively attach to “jemna” across a name without je</quote> (Section 10.20). Here “meris” is a name, not a selbri, so “ba meris” cannot form “will Meris”; names cannot function as predicates. The intended meaning “will compete with Meris” requires “je ba jemna ba meris” or explicit connectives, not this conflation.  
   c. Ambiguous Pro-sumti Assignment  
      – If “jemna” is the predicate and mi’o is x1, then “ba meris” at x2 means “we will compete with Meris,” but then the vocative “doi jemna” is nonsensical: one cannot address “O competitor” and then speak about “we” competing with Meris. If instead “jemna” is vocative, then the predicate and sumti roles collapse. Without explicit pro-sumti or clarifying abstraction (e.g., ku…ku’e), x-place assignment is ambiguous and unlicensed (Section 7.2).  

4. Objections to Debater_A’s Arguments  
   a. Misuse of Pro-sumti Anaphora Across Sentences  
      – Debater_A claims “e” covers omitted sumti across utterances. However, <quote>“e” is implicit only within a bridi, not across sentence boundaries”</quote> (Section 7.16). They never employ anaphoric linkers like je or vau.  
   b. Invalid Name-as-Predicate in (B)  
      – They argue “ba meris” is “will go to Meris” as if turning Meris into a location. But “meris” is a person’s name (cmene), not a place or event; without conversion (e.g., le cmene be meris), it cannot act as selbri. They ignore the need for ku…ku’e or conversion constructs (Section 19.17).  
   c. Overreliance on Ellipsis and Context  
      – A sentence must be grammatical on its own. Both (A) and (B) rely on ellipsis of sumti, terminators, and connectives that the grammar does not permit to be elided. Valid Lojban demands explicit markers when deviating from the most basic form.
